title: Cloud Foundations for IT Managers
description: A five-module short course on how public cloud services are structured, secured, priced and provisioned, written for people who manage technology decisions rather than write code.

items.title: IaaS, PaaS, SaaS and who is responsible for what
items.body:
Public cloud providers sell computing at three broad levels. Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS) rents virtual machines, block storage and networks; you install and patch the operating system and everything above it. Platform as a Service (PaaS) runs your application on a managed runtime or database; the provider patches the platform and you supply code and data. Software as a Service (SaaS) delivers a finished application over the web; you configure it and manage your users.

The shared responsibility model describes the split. The provider is always responsible for the security of the cloud: the physical facilities, the hardware, the hypervisor and the provider-managed software. The customer is responsible for security in the cloud: identities and access, data classification and encryption choices, network rules, and — for IaaS — the guest operating system and applications. The line moves upward as you move from IaaS to SaaS, but it never disappears: even in SaaS you still own who can log in, what they can see and whether multi-factor authentication is enforced.

For a manager the practical consequence is that a contract with a provider does not transfer accountability. Data-protection obligations, access reviews and backup verification remain yours, and audits will ask for evidence of them. The most common cloud incidents are not provider outages but misconfigured customer-side permissions and storage exposed to the public internet — failures on the customer's side of the line.

items.title: Geography as an architecture decision
items.body:
A region is a geographic area containing several availability zones. An availability zone is one or more data centres with independent power, cooling and networking, connected to the other zones in the region by low-latency links. Zones are far enough apart that a fire or flood should not take two down at once, but close enough that an application can run across them synchronously.

Resilience is bought in tiers. Running one server in one zone means a zone failure is an outage. Running copies across two or three zones behind a load balancer survives a zone failure, and most managed databases offer a standby in a second zone that takes over automatically. Running in two regions protects against a regional event, but it is expensive: data must be replicated over long distances, replication is usually asynchronous, and failover has to be rehearsed or it will not work.

The manager's questions are about targets. The recovery time objective (RTO) is how long the service may be down; the recovery point objective (RPO) is how much data may be lost. A multi-zone design commonly gives an RTO of minutes and an RPO near zero. A cross-region design with asynchronous replication gives an RPO of seconds to minutes and an RTO that depends entirely on how automated and how well tested the failover is. Data residency rules — where personal data may be stored — often decide the region before performance does.

items.prompt: An availability zone is best described as:
choices: One or more data centres with independent power and networking inside a region

items.prompt: Recovery point objective (RPO) measures:
choices: Acceptable data loss, measured in time

items.title: Identities, roles and the blast radius of a credential
items.body:
Every action in a cloud account is an API call made by an identity: a person, a service, or a piece of automation. Access is granted by attaching policies that list allowed actions on named resources. Least privilege means each identity is allowed only the actions its job requires, on only the resources it needs, and nothing more.

The root or owner account of a subscription can do anything and should be used almost never; it belongs in a safe with hardware multi-factor authentication. Day-to-day work should happen through named accounts federated from the organisation's identity provider, with roles assumed for specific tasks and time-limited credentials rather than long-lived keys. Long-lived access keys stored in code repositories are the single most common cause of cloud account compromise reported by providers, and an exposed key with broad permissions can run up large bills within hours.

A manager should expect three controls to exist and to be evidenced: multi-factor authentication for every human account, periodic access reviews that remove unused permissions, and an audit log of API calls retained where administrators cannot alter it. The blast radius of a compromised credential is set by the permissions attached to it, so the review question is not 'who has access' but 'what could this identity do if it were stolen'.

items.prompt: Least privilege means an identity is allowed:
choices: All actions in its own account
Only the actions and resources its job requires

items.prompt: The root/owner account should be:
choices: Reserved, protected with hardware MFA and rarely used

items.prompt: The most common cause of cloud account compromise cited in the reading is:
choices: Long-lived access keys exposed in code

items.prompt: Blast radius of a stolen credential is determined by:
choices: The region it was created in

items.title: On-demand, commitments and spot
items.body:
Cloud compute is priced three ways. On-demand charges by the second or hour with no commitment and the highest unit price. Commitments — reserved instances, savings plans, committed-use discounts — trade a one- or three-year promise for a lower rate, typically tens of percent off, and suit steady baseline load. Spot or preemptible capacity is spare provider capacity sold at a deep discount that can be reclaimed at short notice; it suits batch work and anything that can be interrupted.

Storage, data transfer and managed services have their own meters. Data leaving the provider's network (egress) is charged per gigabyte and is the line item most often underestimated. Managed databases and serverless functions bill on requests, duration and provisioned capacity, so the shape of the workload matters more than its size.

Cost control is an operating discipline, not a purchase. Budgets with alerts, tags that attribute every resource to an owner and a purpose, regular review of idle and oversized resources, and commitments sized to measured baseline usage are the four practices that keep bills predictable. The FinOps Foundation's FOCUS specification defines a common billing-export format across providers, which makes the review comparable when more than one cloud is in use.

items.title: Why the infrastructure should be a file
items.body:
Infrastructure as code (IaC) describes cloud resources in files that a tool turns into API calls. Declarative tools such as Terraform and CloudFormation describe the desired end state; the tool computes the difference from the current state and applies it. The files live in version control, so every change has an author, a review and a history, and an environment can be rebuilt from scratch.

The management benefits are review and repeatability. A change to a firewall rule arrives as a pull request that a second person reads before it is applied; a plan step shows exactly what will be created, changed or destroyed. Policy-as-code scanners can reject a change that opens a storage bucket to the public before it reaches an account. Drift — manual changes made in a console — is detected when the next plan shows differences the files do not explain.

The cost is discipline. State files must be stored securely and locked during changes; secrets must never be written into the files; and the console must become read-only for the environments the code manages, or the two will diverge. Teams that adopt IaC without those rules get the tooling without the benefit.

items.prompt: A declarative IaC tool works by:
choices: Computing the difference between desired and current state and applying it

items.prompt: Drift is:
choices: Manual changes that diverge from the code

items.prompt: Which must never be written into IaC files?
The plan step exists to:
choices: Show what will be created, changed or destroyed before applying
